blocks.text: This process is used to separate one of the components of a two-component heterogeneous mixture from a solution. The first step is to select a suitable solvent in which one of the components dissolves completely while the other remains practically insoluble. For example, let us take a mixture of common salt and sand.
Dissolve this mixture in distilled water. The common salt will distribute itself through out water to give a homogeneous mixture. This homogenous mixture is called a solution of common salt in water.

blocks.alt: A hand pours a liquid mixture from a tilted beaker down a glass rod into a glass funnel lined with filter paper. The funnel is held by a clamp on a stand, and drops of filtrate fall into a beaker below.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.1: The process of filtration (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.1).

blocks.text: Common salt in this solution is called a solute while water is called a solvent. In a solution, the solvent is that component which is present in excess as compared to the solute. While common salt disappears in water, the other component, sand remains undissolved and after some time settles down at the bottom of solution.

The process of filtration is used to separate sand from the above solution. It can be performed with several types of filter media. Nature of the precipitate and other factors dictate which filter medium must be used. The most convenient ways of filtration are either through a filter paper or through a filter crucible.
Folding of filter paper is important and is done in two ways.

1. Filtration by a glass funnel and filter paper is usually a slow process. As the mixture is poured onto the filter paper, the solvent (water) passes through leaving behind the suspended particles on the filter paper. Filter papers are available in a variety of porosites (pore sizes). Which pore size is to be used, depends upon the size of particles in the precipitate. The filter paper should be large enough so that it is one-fourth to one-half full of precipitate at the end of filtration. In this way, the filtrate runs down the side of beaker without splashing. A complete filtration assembly is shown in Figure 15.1.

blocks.alt: Three drawings: a round filter paper with a dashed line down the middle (first fold), the half circle with a dashed line across it (second fold), and the paper opened into a cone (forming the cone).
blocks.caption: Figure 15.2a: Folding of filtration paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.2a).

blocks.text: The folded filter paper may then be inserted into 60-degree funnel, moistened with water and firmly pressed down.

2. The rate of filtration through conical funnel can be considerably increased using a Fluted Filter Paper, for preparation of such a paper ordinary filter paper in folded in such a way that a fan like arrangement with alternate elevations and depressions at various folds is obtained Fig (15.2 b).

blocks.alt: Seven steps: filter disk; fold in half; fold in half again; fold to crease the quarter section; fold to crease the eight section; the pleated accordion shape; open filter cone.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.2b: Fluted filter paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.2b).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed caption reads 'Fluttled filter paper'; the correct word is fluted.
After filtration, the liquid which is obtained in the conical flask underneath the funnel is called the filtrate. The sand left behind on the funnel is called the residue.
Another convenient way to filter a precipitate is by suction through a crucible. Two types of crucibles are generally used.

1. Gooch crucible is made of porcelain having a perforated bottom which is covered with paper pulp or a filter paper cut to its size as shown in Figure 15.3. Quick filtration can be done by placing such crucible in a suction filtering apparatus. It is useful for the filtration of precipitates, which need to be ignited at high temperature. If its perforations are covered with asbestos mat, it may be used to filter solutions that react with paper e.g. concentrated HCl and KMnO₄ solutions.

blocks.alt: A white porcelain crucible turned upside down to show its bottom full of small holes, with a loose perforated disc and a round plate beside it.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.3: Gooch crucible (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.3).

blocks.alt: A glass crucible with a white porous glass disc sealed across its lower part.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.4: Sintered glass crucible (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.4).

blocks.text: 2. Sintered glass crucible is a glass crucible with a porous glass disc sealed into the bottom. It is very convenient to use because no preparation is needed as with the Gooch crucible as shown in Figure 15.4.
